title: Good components of a semilinear Sylow quotient
statement: Let $e$ be a field, $\ell$ a prime different from $\operatorname{char}(e)$, and $K/e$ a finite field extension [def-weil-field] [def-pc-field-extension]. Let a finite group $G$ act on $K$ by $e$-automorphisms with $K^G/e$ purely inseparable. Let $B$ be a nonempty normal proper finite-type $e$-scheme, a finite disjoint union of integral schemes, and let $Y$ be a smooth projective $K$-scheme [def-pc-integral-scheme] [def-weil-proper-morphism] [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms] [def-kun-projective]. Let $G$ act on $Y$ by $e$-automorphisms, equivariantly for $Y\to\operatorname{Spec}K$. Suppose an invariant projective surjection $h:Y\to B$ sends generic points to generic points with finite residue extensions, all subgroup quotients exist as finite geometric categorical scheme quotients with invariant structure sheaves, and over a dense open meeting every component of $B$ the induced map $Y/G\to B$ is a finite universal homeomorphism [def-trf-projective-bundle-morphism] [def-weil-surjective-morphism] [def-weil-finite-integral-morphism] [def-weil-universal-homeomorphism]. Fix an $\ell$-Sylow subgroup $L\leq G$, namely a subgroup of $\ell$-power order and index prime to $\ell$. Set $F=K^L$ and $Q=Y/L$. Then $[F:e]$ is prime to $\ell$, and $K/F$ is finite Galois with Galois group the image of $L$ in $\operatorname{Aut}_e(K)$. There is an open and closed union $Q^\circ$ of irreducible components of $Q$, meeting the fibre over every generic point of $B$, such that $Q^\circ$ is normal projective over $F$, the induced $d:Q^\circ\to B$ is projective surjective and sends all its generic points to generic points of $B$, and all their residue-field extensions are finite of degree prime to $\ell$ [def-weil-irreducible-components] [def-sc-generic-point] [def-weil-residue-field]. Its inverse image $Y^\circ\subseteq Y$ is open and closed and $Y^\circ\to Q^\circ$ is the finite quotient by $L$. Normal means that every local ring is an integrally closed domain. Purely inseparable means that every element has a power of the characteristic in the smaller field (and the extension is trivial in characteristic zero); finite Galois means finite, normal and separable. The assertion does not require the omitted components of $Q$ to have prime-to-$\ell$ residue degree. Field-extension terminology and degrees are as in [def-pc-field-tower].

source.place: Expose X 2.3 Step 2, diagram (2.c), printed p.151, with explicit selection of components for the every-generic-point degree convention. The selection uses Sylow conjugacy in each decomposition group and invariant-field degrees, rather than interpreting a total degree as each residue degree.

proof.text: Put $E=K^G$, $H=\operatorname{im}(G\to\operatorname{Aut}_eK)$ and $J=\operatorname{im}(L\to\operatorname{Aut}_eK)$. These image groups act faithfully. The finite-field-action theorem gives $[K:E]=|H|$ and $[K:F]=|J|$, and makes $K/F$ finite Galois. Its automorphism group has order $[K:F]=|J|$ by the finite-Galois theorem, so the inclusion of $J$ into that group is equality. This proves the asserted Galois-group clause without assuming the original action of $L$ faithful.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2, printed p.151: K/K^L, with the kernel of the constants action removed.

proof.text: Let $N=\ker(G\to H)$. Counting cosets gives $[G:L]=[H:J][N:N\cap L]$: the map $G/L\to H/J$ is onto and each fibre has cardinal $[N:N\cap L]$. Thus $[H:J]$ is prime to $\ell$. The degree tower $E\subseteq F\subseteq K$ gives $[F:E]=|H|/|J|=[H:J]$. In positive characteristic $p$, the finite purely inseparable extension $E/e$ is normal (each minimal polynomial has only its one root), and has exactly one embedding into an algebraic closure; the normal-field-degree-factors theorem therefore makes $[E:e]$ a power of $p$. In characteristic zero $E=e$ by the meaning of purely inseparable. As $p\ne\ell$, the second degree tower gives $[F:e]=[F:E][E:e]$ prime to $\ell$. All towers are finite since their fields lie in the given finite extension $K/e$.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2, printed p.151: the prime-to-ell constants degree; inseparable degree is a characteristic power (Stacks 09HI).

proof.text: Smoothness over $K$ makes $Y$ regular and locally Noetherian, hence normal. Projectivity makes $Y/K$ proper, hence finite type; since a field is Noetherian, the finite-type theorem makes $Y$ Noetherian. The normal-component theorem decomposes $Y$ as a finite disjoint union of open-and-closed normal integral components. This applies even when the components are not geometrically integral.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2, printed p.151: normality and components of the smooth projective model; Stacks 056S, 033M.

proof.text: For $k=e$ and for $k=F$, the morphism $\operatorname{Spec}K\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is finite because $K/k$ is finite-dimensional. The finite-projective-bundle theorem followed by the ample-base conversion makes it H-projective: the trivial line on $\operatorname{Spec}k$ is ample, since its unit section has the whole affine scheme as nonvanishing locus. Compose with the given H-projective $Y/K$ to obtain $Y/k$ H-projective, hence proper. The invariant map $Y\to\operatorname{Spec}F$ descends by the categorical property of $q_L$, and gives $Q$ its $F$-structure; the descended map agrees with the original $e$-structure. Likewise the $G$-invariant structure map $Y\to\operatorname{Spec}e$ descends through $q_G$ and gives $Z=Y/G$ its $e$-structure, so $q_G$ is a morphism of $e$-schemes and $q_L$ a morphism of $F$-schemes; uniqueness in the categorical property shows that an invariant $e$- (resp. $F$-)morphism factors through a morphism of $e$- (resp. $F$-)schemes. Apply the normal-proper-quotient lemma to $(Y,G,e)$ and $(Y,L,F)$. Thus $Z=Y/G$ is normal proper finite type over $e$, and $Q=Y/L$ is normal proper finite type over $F$; both are Noetherian.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2, diagram (2.c), printed p.151. Constants descent by the assumed categorical quotient; finite structural maps are projective by Stacks 0B3I and 087S.

proof.text: Decompose $Q$ into its finitely many clopen normal integral components $C$. For each $C$, its inverse image $X_C=q_L^{-1}C$ is clopen in $Y$. A clopen subscheme is also a closed subscheme, as the defining ideal is zero on it and the unit ideal on its complement. Compose this closed inclusion with a projective embedding of $Y/F$ to obtain a projective embedding of $X_C/F$, and hence an ample invertible sheaf on $X_C$. The restricted map $X_C\to C$ is finite surjective: on an affine open of $C$ it is the same finite algebra as for $q_L$. Apply finite-normal ample descent to obtain an ample invertible sheaf on $C$. Glue these sheaves on the disjoint components to an invertible sheaf on $Q$. It is ample: extend an affine-nonvanishing section on a chosen component by zero on all other components; its nonvanishing locus is the original affine open. Quasi-compactness holds because there are finitely many components. This uses the definition of ample, without descending a chosen linearization.

source.place: Tag 0BD4(2), applied to each normal integral target component; finite disjoint gluing of ample sheaves is the defining affine-nonvanishing criterion.

proof.text: The ample-immersion theorem, applicable since $Q/F$ is finite type, gives an immersion $Q\to\mathbf P^n_F$. The target is separated over $F$ and $Q$ is proper over $F$, so the proper-to-separated-target theorem makes the immersion proper. A proper immersion is closed. Thus $Q$ is projective over $F$ in the required finite-projective-space convention.

source.place: Tags 01VS and 01VT (ample immersion over an affine base), Constructions 01NH (projective space separated), 01W6 (map from a proper scheme to a separated target), and Schemes 01IQ (immersion with closed image is closed).

proof.text: Fix a generic point $b$ of $B$. It lies in the specified dense open $U$. The finite universal homeomorphism $Z_U\to U$ has exactly one point $t$ over $b$, which is generic: on the component containing $b$ it is a homeomorphism. Its residue extension $T=\kappa(t)/\kappa(b)$ is finite by finiteness of this morphism and purely inseparable because a universal homeomorphism is universally injective, hence radicial. The generic-field comparison for $q_G:Y\to Z$ identifies the components above $t$ as one $G$-orbit. Choose a generic point $\eta$ in this orbit, put $M=\kappa(\eta)$ and $D=\operatorname{Stab}_G(\eta)$. The same comparison gives $T=M^D$ with its canonical embedding in $M$. All components of $Z$ meet $Z_U$: every generic of $Y$ maps to a generic of $B$ by hypothesis, and the quotient comparison maps these onto the generic points of $Z$.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2, printed p.151: the dense-open radicial quotient. Generic-field identification is applied without freeness; Stacks 01S4 gives inseparable residue extensions.

proof.text: Choose an $\ell$-Sylow subgroup $P$ of the finite stabilizer $D$. Regard $P$ as an $\ell$-subgroup of $G$ and apply Sylow conjugate containment to obtain $g$ with $gPg^{-1}\subseteq L$. Replace $\eta$ by $\eta'=g\eta$, and write $D'=gDg^{-1}$ and $M'=\kappa(\eta')$. Put $S=D'\cap L$. It contains the $\ell$-Sylow subgroup $gPg^{-1}$ of $D'$, while it is itself an $\ell$-group as a subgroup of $L$. Hence $|S|=|P|$ and $[D':S]$ is prime to $\ell$. The point $\eta'$ still maps to $b$ because $h$ is invariant. This chooses a conjugate separately for this generic point of $B$, rather than imposing a simultaneous containment on all stabilizers.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2, printed p.151, explicit stabilizer-wise Sylow selection for the all-generic-points convention.

proof.text: Let $c=q_L(\eta')$, a generic point of $Q$. The quotient comparison gives $\kappa(c)=(M')^S$ and $T=(M')^{D'}$. Let $A$ and $A_0$ be the images of $D'$ and $S$ in $\operatorname{Aut}(M')$. The faithful finite-action theorem gives $[M':T]=|A|$ and $[M':\kappa(c)]=|A_0|$. The tower law gives $[\kappa(c):T]=[A:A_0]$. Counting fibres of $D'/S\to A/A_0$ shows that this index divides $[D':S]$, so it is prime to $\ell$. Since $T/\kappa(b)$ is finite purely inseparable, its degree is a characteristic power (or one in characteristic zero), by the normal-field-degree-factors theorem as in step 2. Multiplying degrees now proves that $[\kappa(c):\kappa(b)]$ is finite and prime to $\ell$. The field-action theorem is applied to image groups, so generic inertia is allowed.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2, diagram (2.c), printed p.151: intermediate invariant-field degrees, with decomposition groups and possible generic inertia made explicit.

proof.text: Do this for each of the finitely many generic points $b$ of $B$, choosing one resulting component of $Q$ over each. Let $Q^\circ$ be the union of those components. By the normal-component theorem it is open and closed, normal, and its generic points are precisely the finitely many selected generic points; each has the finite prime-to-$\ell$ residue degree proved in step 9. It meets every generic fibre of $B$. Its closed inclusion into the projective $F$-scheme $Q$, composed with the projective embedding of $Q$, makes $Q^\circ/F$ projective. No condition is inferred for any component omitted from this union.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2, printed p.151, retaining good components for the every-generic-point definition of prime-to-ell alteration.

proof.text: The finite map $\operatorname{Spec}F\to\operatorname{Spec}e$ is H-projective by the finite-projective-bundle theorem and the ample-base conversion, again using the unit section of the trivial line on the affine base. Composition therefore gives a closed immersion $i:Q^\circ\hookrightarrow\mathbf P^N_e$. Let $d:Q^\circ\to B$ be the descended map, restricted to this union. The diagonal of $B/e$ is closed because $B/e$ is proper. Its base change is the graph $Q^\circ\to Q^\circ\times_eB$, so the graph is closed. The map $Q^\circ\times_eB\to\mathbf P^N_e\times_eB$ is the base change of $i$, hence closed. Their composite is a closed immersion over $B$, exhibiting $d$ as H-projective, and thus also projective in the projective-bundle convention (the ambient bundle is that of $\mathcal O_B^{N+1}$).

source.place: Tags 0B3I, 087S, 01W9 for finite structural maps and projective composition; closed graph is base change of the diagonal, with closed immersions stable under base change and composition.

proof.text: Projectivity makes $d$ proper, so its image is closed by the definition of universally closed applied to the identity base change. This image contains every generic point of $B$ by construction. A closed subset containing the generic point of every irreducible component contains every component, so the image is all of $B$. Thus $d$ is surjective. The generic-point and residue-degree clauses were established for every component retained in $Q^\circ$, not just for their total degree.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2, printed p.151: proper dominant components give the desired projective surjection.

proof.text: Set $Y^\circ=q_L^{-1}(Q^\circ)$. It is clopen and $L$-stable. The restricted quotient is finite and surjective, has the same orbit geometric fibres, and has invariant structure sheaf by restricting the corresponding statements for $q_L$ to the open $Q^\circ$; on each affine open the same finite algebra occurs. Its categorical property can be checked directly. Given an invariant morphism $f:Y^\circ\to T$, extend it on the disjoint complement by $q_L$ to obtain an invariant map $Y\to T\amalg(Q\setminus Q^\circ)$. Descend it through $q_L$, then restrict to $Q^\circ$: surjectivity on points forces this restriction to land in the summand $T$. This gives the required factorization; uniqueness follows either from the categorical uniqueness for the extended map or from that same descent construction. Hence $Y^\circ\to Q^\circ$ is the finite quotient by $L$ claimed in the statement.

source.place: X 2.3 Step 2, printed p.151: restriction to the selected clopen union; categorical restriction proved by extension to a disjoint-union target.
